subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: From Cave Tallies to the Snakes-and-Ladders Board

tasks_in_class.description: Look at the picture. Estimate and write the number of each of the following objects: (a) Oranges (b) Bangles (c) Laddoos (d) Barfi (e) Bindis (f) Bananas.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Play (fill missing numbers), p.17
tasks_in_class.description: Fill the missing numbers on the snakes and ladders board.
You are standing on 96. Which number on the die will take you to the snake's mouth?
Show the number written on the tail of the longest snake using bundles and loose sticks.

time_bands.activity: The teacher tells the short story of how humans counted — cave tallies, groups of five and ten, up to the ancient Indian ten-symbol invention and the special role of zero as a place-holder. Students listen and respond to the question: what is different about the Indian system from a tally?

Let us Do Q1, p.16 ("Look at the picture. Estimate and write the number....") — Students study the illustrated bazaar and write their estimates for oranges, bangles, laddoos, barfi, bindis, and bananas. Pairs share and discuss how they formed each estimate.

Let us Play (fill missing numbers), p.17 ("Fill the missing numbers on the snakes and ladders board.") — Students work individually to complete the partly-filled board, reinforcing the sequence 1–100.

Let us Play Q3, p.17 ("You are standing on 96. Which number on the die....") — The class reasons aloud about which die value reaches the snake's mouth. Let us Play Q4, p.17 ("Show the number written on the tail of the longest snake....") — Students represent that number with bundled sticks drawn on paper.

periods.teacher_notes: The historical narrative anchors the abstract idea of place value and zero in human story — ask students what problem zero solves rather than stating it. For the bazaar estimation, accept a range of reasonable answers and praise the reasoning, not the exact figure. A common error is confusing the tail and the mouth of a snake when navigating the board; reinforce that snakes take you down from mouth to tail.
materials: Bundled matchstick sticks or drawn stick-bundle sketches

periods.activity_title: Making 100 — Bundles, Jumps, and Talking Pot

tasks_in_class.description: Complete the Talking Pot exchanges: I said 39, Pot said ___; I said ___, Pot said 90; I said 63, Pot said ___; I said ___, Pot said ___.
Fill in the blanks: use matchstick bundles (Making 100 table) and draw jumps on the number line to show 65+35=100 and make 100 by different jumps.
Use matchstick bundles and a ginladi to make 100 in different ways. Fill the table: 60 and 40 makes ___, 45 and ___ makes 100, ___ and 25 makes 100, ___ and 85 makes 100.
Write numbers in the blank spaces inside the flower petals so that the numbers in each petal add up to 100.

time_bands.activity: Let us Think (Talking Pot), p.18 ("Complete the Talking Pot exchanges: I said 39, Pot said....") — The teacher introduces the Talking Pot character and its rule (always says the successor). Students complete the four exchanges in pairs and share their reasoning.

Let us Do Q1, p.19 ("Fill in the blanks: use matchstick bundles... and draw jumps....") — Students use ten bundles of ten matchsticks to concretely build 100, then draw the complementary jump (65+35) on the number line. Several different jump-pairs are shared with the class.

Let us Do Q2, p.19 ("Use matchstick bundles and a ginladi to make 100 in different ways....") — Students manipulate bundles on the desk and record pairs that total 100 in the table (60+40, 45+55, 75+25, 15+85).

Let us Do Q3, p.20 ("Write numbers in the blank spaces inside the flower petals so that the numbers....") — Students fill the petal diagram, then explain to a partner how they found each missing addend.

periods.teacher_notes: Emphasise that 10 bundles of 10 sticks each is the same as 100 single sticks — this concrete grouping is the foundation for the hundreds place. A common error is students treating the Talking Pot as doubling rather than adding 1; confirm the rule explicitly at the start. The exploration tasks T-11 and T-12 (matchbox count and seed handful) are rich hands-on extensions; include them if class pace allows, or suggest them as a family activity.
materials: Ginladi / abacus tool or drawn substitute

periods.activity_title: Estimating and Counting — Getting Close to 100

tasks_in_class.description: Open a full box of matchsticks. Estimate the number, count them, check how close your estimate was, and find how many boxes get close to 100 matchsticks.
Take a handful of seeds (kidney beans, chickpeas). Estimate the number, count them, and find how many handfuls get close to 100 seeds.

time_bands.activity: Building on the idea that ten bundles of ten sticks make 100, the teacher distributes one matchbox per group. Students examine the box, write their estimate on a slip, then open it and arrange sticks in bundles of ten to count accurately. Groups record: estimate, actual count, and difference.

Let us Explore Q1, p.20 ("Open a full box of matchsticks. Estimate the number, count them, check how close....") — Groups determine how many such boxes would be needed to reach 100 matchsticks and record their reasoning in writing.

Let us Explore Q2, p.20 ("Take a handful of seeds (kidney beans, chickpeas). Estimate the number, count them....") — Each student takes a handful of seeds, writes an estimate, counts in groups of ten, and works out how many handfuls approach 100. Groups share their figures and note the variation.
A quick round-up: the teacher asks two or three groups to share the gap between their estimate and actual count. The class briefly discusses why estimating by grouping in tens helps accuracy.

periods.teacher_notes: Grouping in tens before counting is the key habit to build; circulate and prompt any group counting one-by-one to re-organise into bundles of ten first. A common error is students fixing their estimate after counting — insist estimates are written before the box or handful is counted. Comparing how many boxes or handfuls reach 100 links back to the idea of 100 as a landmark quantity, reinforced in the complementary-pairs work of the previous unit on this section.
materials: Seeds — kidney beans or chickpeas (a cup per group)
Small slips of paper for estimates

section_titles: Numbers from 100 to 150 — Place Value H-T-O
periods.activity_title: Beyond 100 — Reading and Building Three-Digit Numbers

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do (fill table 101–110 + number line), p.21
tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the blank spaces in the table (100 and 1 makes ___… 100 and 10 makes 110 — number names and numerals) and fill the number line from 100 to 124.
Identify bundles and loose sticks in the H-T-O matchstick table and write the corresponding numbers. Extend the table in your notebook till 150.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do (match numbers to bundles), p.23
tasks_in_class.description: Match the numbers 101, 116, 110, 100, 140 with the correct bundles and loose sticks.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do (fill table 101–110 + number line), p.21 ("Fill in the blank spaces in the table (100 and 1 makes ___....") — The teacher introduces the idea of one hundred bundle as the H column. Students fill the table from 101 to 110, writing both numeral and number name, then complete the number line from 100 to 124.

Let us Do Q1, p.22 ("Identify bundles and loose sticks in the H-T-O matchstick table and write the corresponding numbers....") — Students read the H-T-O table, identify what each column of bundles represents, write the numbers, and then extend the table to 150 in their notebooks.

Let us Do (match numbers to bundles), p.23 ("Match the numbers 101, 116, 110, 100, 140 with the correct bundles....") — Students draw lines from each numeral to its bundle picture. The teacher checks a few responses aloud and highlights how the H column always holds the hundred-bundle.

periods.teacher_notes: Stress that the H column always contains exactly one large bundle of 100, while T and O follow the familiar tens-and-ones structure — this prevents students from treating three-digit numbers as merely 'big two-digit numbers'. A common error is writing 100+16 as 116 but drawing only 16 sticks, ignoring the hundred bundle; reinforce the three-column structure with physical bundles. Talking Pot task T-16 and number-line task T-17 are rich follow-ups noted below for additional practice.
materials: Matchstick bundles (including one large bundle of 100)

section_titles: Numbers from 100 to 150 — Place Value H-T-O

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do (number line 100–150 + show numbers), p.23
tasks_in_class.description: Fill blank spaces on the number line (100–150). Show: place an arrow on 125, make a tree on 112, make a smiley on 149, put a cross on 137.

time_bands.activity: Let us Think (Talking Pot 127–150), p.23 ("Complete the Talking Pot table: 127→128, 109→___, 134→___, 105→___, ___→150, 100→___....") — Students complete the successor table individually. The teacher draws attention to the crossing from 109 to 110 (tens digit changes) and 149 to 150 (tens and ones both reset or advance).

Let us Do (number line 100–150 + show numbers), p.23 ("Fill blank spaces on the number line (100–150). Show: place an arrow on 125....") — Students fill the number line, then place each of the four symbols at their correct positions. Pairs check each other's placement and discuss any disagreement.

periods.teacher_notes: The Talking Pot successor exercise is particularly valuable at the 109→110 transition, where ones digit reaches 9 and both tens and ones change — highlight this pattern and ask students to predict what happens at 119 and 139. A common error on the number line is placing 125 closer to 120 or to 130 without counting intervals; encourage students to mark every tenth first (110, 120, 130…) before pinpointing individual numbers. Additional practice: Let us Do (match numbers to bundles), p.23 items for any students who finish early.

section_titles: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
periods.activity_title: Clap, Snap, Pat — Encoding Place Value with the Body

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Play (Clap, Snap and Pat), p.24
tasks_in_class.description: Play in two teams: one team shows a three-digit number using clap (100), snap (10), and pat (1); the other team guesses the number.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do (table 150–159, extend to 200), p.24
tasks_in_class.description: Fill the blank spaces in the counting table from 150 to 159 (pictorial form, matchstick bundles, number sentence, number name). Extend to 200 in your notebook.
Draw jumps of 5 on the number line (100–150) and write the numbers in the given spaces.

homework.book_ref: Let us Do at Home, p.25
homework.description: Fill a small container with seeds. Estimate how many seeds are in it, count them, then guess how many container-fills get close to 200 seeds.

time_bands.activity: Let us Play (Clap, Snap and Pat), p.24 ("Play in two teams: one team shows a three-digit number using clap (100), snap (10), and pat (1)....") — Teams take turns encoding and decoding numbers in the range 150–200. The teacher calls out a number for the encoding team and the decoding team writes the numeral.

Let us Do (table 150–159, extend to 200), p.24 ("Fill the blank spaces in the counting table from 150 to 159....") — Students complete the four-column table (pictorial form, matchstick bundles, number sentence, number name) for 150–159, then extend the pattern to 200 in their notebooks.

Let us Do Q1, p.26 ("Draw jumps of 5 on the number line (100–150) and write the numbers....") — Students draw arcs of 5 along the number line and label each landing point, practising skip-counting by 5 within the range 100–150.

periods.teacher_notes: The Clap-Snap-Pat game ties place-value columns to a physical, memorable rhythm; ensure each clap is deliberate so students map one clap = one hundred clearly before the guessing begins. A common error in the counting table is writing 159, 160, 161 correctly in numerals but then drawing only 5 ten-bundles (instead of 6) for 160 — reinforce that a new ten-bundle appears when ones reach 10. The home exploration with seeds is set as homework to bring the 200-landmark alive concretely.

section_titles: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation

tasks_in_class.description: Continue the jumps of 20 and write the missing numbers on the number line (100–200).
Fill in the 1-less/number/1-more table for 160, 129, 187, 134, 158.
Show at least two different ways of making the following numbers: (a) use matchstick bundles to make 125; (b) make 145 using a ginladi; (c) make 170 on a number line.

homework.book_ref: Let us Do at Home (stones), p.25
homework.description: Write the numbers in order on the stones (150…158…163…167…177…182…189…199).

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q2, p.26 ("Continue the jumps of 20 and write the missing numbers on the number line (100–200)....") — Students extend the jump-of-20 pattern across the full 100–200 range, labelling each landing. A quick class discussion identifies the pattern in the ones digit across jumps.

Let us Do Q3, p.26 ("Fill in the 1-less/number/1-more table for 160, 129, 187, 134, 158....") — Students complete the three-column table. The teacher draws attention to the entries around 129 (128, 129, 130) and 187 (186, 187, 188), where tens or hundreds digits shift.

Let us Do Q4, p.27 ("Show at least two different ways of making the following numbers: (a) matchstick bundles to make 125....") — Students represent 125 with bundles, 145 on the ginladi, and 170 on a number line. They are encouraged to attempt a second representation for each and share one with a partner.

periods.teacher_notes: When students jump by 20 on the 100–200 number line, ask them to articulate which digit is changing with each jump — this builds the understanding that adding 20 always increases the tens digit by 2. A common error in the 1-less/1-more table is treating 129+1 as 120 by incorrectly rolling tens; have students verify by counting on one from 129 rather than reasoning in their heads. The multi-representation task is deliberately open — celebrate any valid second representation, including a number sentence.

tasks_in_class.description: Fill the empty boxes in the multi-representation table (number, pictorial form, matchstick bundles, number sentence) for 114, 132, a pictorial form, 172, 108, 30 more than 150, and 160.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q5, p.27 ("Fill the empty boxes in the multi-representation table (number, pictorial form, matchstick bundles, number sentence)....") — Students complete all four representations for each row. The teacher circulates and highlights the '30 more than 150' entry as an additive-reasoning step before completing the table.

Let us Do Q6, p.28 ("Mark the following numbers on the number lines: (a) 109, 112, 124, 134, 146; (b) 155, 163, 178, 189, 198; (c) 125, 142, 153, 174, 199....") — Students mark each set of numbers on three separate number lines. Pairs exchange books and verify placements, discussing any that differ.

periods.teacher_notes: The multi-representation table is a strong consolidation task — watch for students who can write the numeral but leave the pictorial or number-sentence columns blank, and prompt them to draw even a rough H-T-O sketch. A common error on the number lines is crowding or spreading marks unevenly; remind students to estimate the interval size before marking. The '30 more than 150' entry is worth a brief class discussion as it introduces additive language for three-digit numbers.

items.prompt: Draw bundles of ten matchsticks and loose sticks to show that 65 and 35 together make 100. Write the number sentence below your drawing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The drawing shows 6 bundles of ten (representing 60) and 5 loose sticks alongside 3 bundles of ten (representing 30) and 5 loose sticks, giving 10 bundles of ten in total. The number sentence reads 65 + 35 = 100.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Group into bundles of ten: 6 bundles + 3 bundles = 9 bundles, then combine the 5 + 5 loose sticks into one more bundle to reach 10 bundles = 100.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use actual sticks to make and count the bundles before drawing; stretch: ask them to show a second pair that also makes 100.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks: use matchstick bundles (Making 100 table) and draw jumps on the number line to show 65+35=100 and make 100 by different jumps.

items.prompt: Priya opens a box of matchsticks and counts 42 sticks. She wants to collect 100 sticks in all. About how many more boxes like this does she need?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: About 2 more boxes. She already has 42; 42 × 2 = 84, and one more box gives roughly 42 × 3 = 126, which overshoots. Two more boxes gives approximately 42 + 42 + 42 ≈ 126 — that overshoots, so the student needs to reason: 100 − 42 = 58 more sticks, and 58 ÷ 42 ≈ 1.4, so about 1 to 2 more boxes. The best approximate answer from the options is 2 more boxes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the sticks already collected from 100, then estimate how many box-loads fill the remainder.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student thinks one more box (≈42 sticks) is enough to reach 100 from 42, underestimating the shortfall of 58.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not related the number of sticks per box to the shortfall and is guessing an unreasonably large number.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be confusing the number of sticks per bundle (10) with the number of boxes needed, treating the problem as a tens-division.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a number line to mark 42, then hop by 42 to see how many hops reach 100; stretch: ask what if the box had 35 sticks — how many boxes then?

exercise.description: Open a full box of matchsticks. Estimate the number, count them, check how close your estimate was, and find how many boxes get close to 100 matchsticks.

items.section_title: Numbers from 100 to 150 — Place Value H-T-O
items.prompt:
Look at the H-T-O table below. Write the number it shows, then write its number name.

H (hundreds bundles) | T (tens bundles) | O (loose sticks)
1                    | 3                | 4
items.visual_stimulus:
H (hundreds bundles) | T (tens bundles) | O (loose sticks)
1                    | 3                | 4

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The number is 134. Its number name is one hundred and thirty-four.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read each column: 1 hundred = 100, 3 tens = 30, 4 ones = 4; add to get 100 + 30 + 4 = 134.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw the bundles column by column before writing the numeral; stretch: ask the student to write two other numbers that also have 1 in the hundreds place.

exercise.description: Identify bundles and loose sticks in the H-T-O matchstick table and write the corresponding numbers. Extend the table in your notebook till 150.

items.section_title: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
items.prompt: Show the number 163 in two different ways. Use matchstick bundles for one way and a number line for the other. Label each way clearly.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Way 1 (matchstick bundles): 1 large bundle of 100, 6 bundles of 10, and 3 loose sticks, labelled H=1, T=6, O=3. Way 2 (number line): a number line from 160 to 165 (or 150 to 165) with an arrow or mark at 163.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose 163 into 1 hundred, 6 tens, 3 ones for the bundle picture; locate 163 between 160 and 170 on the number line.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student make the bundle representation with actual sticks before drawing it; stretch: ask them to show a third way using a number sentence such as 100 + 60 + 3 = 163.

exercise.description: Show at least two different ways of making the following numbers: (a) use matchstick bundles to make 125; (b) make 145 using a ginladi; (c) make 170 on a number line.

items.prompt: A shopkeeper has a jar of laddoos on the counter. Without counting one by one, which is the best way to estimate how many laddoos are in the jar?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask the shopkeeper to weigh the jar

options.label: B
options.text: Count them one by one very carefully

options.label: C
options.text: Look at a small part you can see clearly, guess how many are there, and use that to estimate the total

options.label: D
options.text: Multiply the price of one laddoo by the total price

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Look at a visible portion, estimate that part, and scale up to the whole — this is the estimation strategy the chapter uses for the bazaar scene.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use a known small part as a reference and scale to the whole group.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not understood estimation as a distinct act from exact counting; they default to precision rather than approximation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is confusing a monetary calculation with a quantity estimate, applying an unrelated procedure.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is substituting a measurement tool (weight) for a number estimate, conflating mass with count.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student first estimate a small group of 10 objects and then talk through scaling before answering; stretch: ask them to explain how close their estimate needs to be for it to be useful.

exercise.description: Look at the picture. Estimate and write the number of each of the following objects: (a) Oranges (b) Bangles (c) Laddoos (d) Barfi (e) Bindis (f) Bananas.

items.prompt:
The Talking Pot always says the number that comes just after what you say. Fill in the blanks:
(a) I said 49, Pot said ___.
(b) I said ___, Pot said 80.
(c) I said 99, Pot said ___.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 1 to find the successor, or subtract 1 to find the number said when the Pot's answer is given.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count forward one step on a number line starting from the given number; stretch: ask what number you would say if the Pot said 110.

exercise.description: Complete the Talking Pot exchanges: I said 39, Pot said ___; I said ___, Pot said 90; I said 63, Pot said ___; I said ___, Pot said ___.

items.prompt: A flower has two petals. The numbers on both petals must add up to 100. One petal shows 45. What number goes on the other petal?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the given petal number from 100: 100 − 45 = 55.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student thinks both petals must be equal, perhaps confusing 'adds to 100' with 'same as the other petal'.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have added 20 instead of subtracting from 100, or confused tens digits.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added 100 to 45 instead of finding the complement, confusing the operation direction.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw a jump from 45 to 100 on a number line and count the jump size; stretch: ask them to write two more petal pairs that add to 100.

exercise.description: Write numbers in the blank spaces inside the flower petals so that the numbers in each petal add up to 100.

items.section_title: Numbers from 100 to 150 — Place Value H-T-O
items.prompt: A bundle picture shows 1 large bundle (100), 1 bundle of ten sticks, and 6 loose sticks. Which number does this picture show?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 116. The large bundle represents 100, the one bundle of ten represents 10, and the 6 loose sticks represent 6: 100 + 10 + 6 = 116.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read each column: H = 1 (100), T = 1 (10), O = 6 (6); add to get 116.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student added the hundred bundle and the loose sticks (100 + 6 = 106) but ignored the tens bundle.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student swapped the tens and ones values, reading 1 loose stick and 6 tens bundles instead of 1 tens bundle and 6 loose sticks.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student ignored the hundreds bundle entirely and combined only tens and ones (1 + 6 = 7, written as 17).

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to point to each bundle type and say its value aloud before writing the numeral; stretch: ask them to draw the bundle picture for 140 and explain what changed.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do (match numbers to bundles), p.23
exercise.description: Match the numbers 101, 116, 110, 100, 140 with the correct bundles and loose sticks.

items.section_title: Numbers from 100 to 150 — Place Value H-T-O
items.prompt:
The Talking Pot always says the number just after what you tell it. Fill in the blanks:
(a) I said 109, Pot said ___.
(b) I said ___, Pot said 135.
(c) I said 149, Pot said ___.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 1 to find the successor, or subtract 1 to find the number when the Pot's response is given.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student place the given number on the 100–150 number line and move one step forward; stretch: ask what number the Pot would say if you told it 199.

items.section_title: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
items.prompt: In the Clap-Snap-Pat game, one clap stands for 100, one snap stands for 10, and one pat stands for 1. A player makes 1 clap, 5 snaps, and 7 pats. What number is this?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 157. One clap = 100, five snaps = 50, seven pats = 7; total = 100 + 50 + 7 = 157.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Assign each action its place-value: claps give hundreds, snaps give tens, pats give ones; add the three parts.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student swapped the tens and ones counts, reading 7 snaps and 5 pats instead of 5 snaps and 7 pats.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student arranged the digits in the wrong order, placing the ones count first instead of the hundreds.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student placed snap and pat counts in the wrong positions, reversing tens and ones after placing the hundreds correctly.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student write H = claps, T = snaps, O = pats in a table before writing the numeral; stretch: ask them to invent a number in the 150–200 range and write out the clap-snap-pat sequence for it.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Play (Clap, Snap and Pat), p.24
exercise.description: Play in two teams: one team shows a three-digit number using clap (100), snap (10), and pat (1); the other team guesses the number.

items.prompt: On a snakes-and-ladders board, the numbers go in order from 1 to 100. The number 56 is missing from the board. Which numbers come just before and just after 56?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 55 and 57. The number just before 56 is 55 (one less) and the number just after is 57 (one more).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract 1 from 56 to get the predecessor (55) and add 1 to get the successor (57).

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student subtracted and added 2 instead of 1, confusing neighbour with the number two steps away.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student moved by tens rather than ones, confusing the neighbour in a row with the number above or below on the board.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student found the correct predecessor but then jumped to the nearest round ten instead of adding 1.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count aloud from 54 and stop at the next three numbers to find the neighbours; stretch: ask what two numbers sit on either side of 99.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Play (fill missing numbers), p.17
exercise.description: Fill the missing numbers on the snakes and ladders board.

items.section_title: Numbers from 100 to 150 — Place Value H-T-O
items.prompt:
Fill in the table below.

Hundreds and ones | Number name | Numeral
100 and 7         | ___         | ___
100 and 9         | ___         | ___
100 and 10        | ___         | ___
items.visual_stimulus:
Hundreds and ones | Number name | Numeral
100 and 7         | ...         | ...
100 and 9         | ...         | ...
100 and 10        | ...         | ...

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 1: one hundred and seven, 107. Row 2: one hundred and nine, 109. Row 3: one hundred and ten, 110.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the ones (or tens) to 100 to form the numeral; then read it aloud as the number name.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a bundle of 100 sticks and loose sticks to physically make each number before writing; stretch: ask them to add two more rows of their own choice between 110 and 120.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do (fill table 101–110 + number line), p.21
exercise.description: Fill in the blank spaces in the table (100 and 1 makes ___… 100 and 10 makes 110 — number names and numerals) and fill the number line from 100 to 124.

items.section_title: Numbers from 100 to 150 — Place Value H-T-O
items.prompt: On a number line from 100 to 150, where would you place the number 138?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Between 130 and 140, closer to 140. Since 138 is 8 steps past 130 and only 2 steps before 140, it sits near the 140 end of that interval.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Locate the tens boundaries on either side of 138 (130 and 140), then judge closeness by counting steps from each boundary.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student placed the number one interval too low, likely misreading 138 as 128 or confusing the 3 in 138 with a pointer to the 120–130 region.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student placed the number in the correct interval but on the wrong side, reversing near and far from 140.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student rounded to the nearest ten but then confused rounding with placement, stopping exactly on 130.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count from 130 up to 138 on their fingers to feel how far 138 is from 130; stretch: ask them to mark 132 and 147 on the same number line and explain their placements.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do (number line 100–150 + show numbers), p.23
exercise.description: Fill blank spaces on the number line (100–150). Show: place an arrow on 125, make a tree on 112, make a smiley on 149, put a cross on 137.

items.section_title: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
items.prompt:
Fill in the blank spaces in the counting table below.

Number | Number name
152    | ___
___    | one hundred and fifty-five
157    | ___
items.visual_stimulus:
Number | Number name
152    | ...
...    | one hundred and fifty-five
157    | ...

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 1: one hundred and fifty-two. Row 2: 155. Row 3: one hundred and fifty-seven.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the numeral as hundreds + tens + ones to form the name, or reverse the name's words into a numeral.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use the textbook counting table (150–159) as a reference to locate the number name pattern; stretch: ask them to extend the table for 158, 159, and 160 in their notebook.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do (table 150–159, extend to 200), p.24
exercise.description: Fill the blank spaces in the counting table from 150 to 159 (pictorial form, matchstick bundles, number sentence, number name). Extend to 200 in your notebook.

items.section_title: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
items.prompt: The table shows a number and its neighbours. Which row is filled correctly?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 174 | 175 | 176. One less than 175 is 174 (175 − 1) and one more is 176 (175 + 1).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract 1 from the number for the left cell and add 1 for the right cell.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student subtracted and added 2 instead of 1, finding the number two away on each side.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student correctly found 1-less (174) but added 2 instead of 1 on the right side.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student reversed the order, placing the larger number on the left and the smaller on the right.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count back one from 175 on their fingers and then count forward one to find each neighbour; stretch: ask them to complete the row for 199 and explain what happens to the hundreds digit for 1-more.

items.section_title: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
items.prompt:
Fill in the empty boxes in the table.

Number | Number sentence      | Number name
___    | 100 + 70 + 2 = ___   | ___
185    | ___                  | ___

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 1: Number = 172; Number sentence = 100 + 70 + 2 = 172; Number name = one hundred and seventy-two. Row 2: Number = 185; Number sentence = 100 + 80 + 5 = 185; Number name = one hundred and eighty-five.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add hundreds, tens, and ones to form the numeral and number name; decompose the numeral into its H-T-O parts for the number sentence.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw the H-T-O bundle picture for each number before writing the number sentence; stretch: ask them to write the number sentence for 30 more than 150 and explain why it equals 180.

items.section_title: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
items.prompt: On a number line from 150 to 200, which letter marks the position of 178?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Between 170 and 180, closer to 180. The number 178 is 8 steps past 170 and only 2 steps before 180.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the tens boundaries on either side of 178 (170 and 180), then count the distance to each boundary.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student placed the number one interval too low, perhaps misreading 178 as 168 or confusing the 7 in 178 with the 160–170 range.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student shifted the number one interval too high, possibly reading 178 as being past 180.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student rounded 178 to 180 and placed it exactly on the round number rather than between marks.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count from 170 to 178 on the number line and note how many steps remain to 180; stretch: ask them to mark 163 and 195 on the same line and explain both placements.
